tier_reason: First-party README table (GET 16B: mrcache 18.6m, redis 2.5m, memcached 400k ops/sec; GET 10kb: 979k, zstd 212k, memcached 261k, redis 313k) with a partial harness (bench/bench.go) but no CPU model, Redis/memcached versions, run command or flags for the runs; the memcached harness is not in the repo. Partial methodology from the project itself is tier C.

corrections.workload: GET of a single small value (16 B) and of a 10 kB value on one node over TCP (almost certainly loopback: 979k ops/sec x 10 kB is about 9.8 GB/s), in-memory; README tables show ops/sec for mrcache, Redis and memcached. The client harness bench/bench.go (Go; defaults 16 connections, 2 s, batch 1, 16-byte key, 256-byte value, one repeated zero-filled key) is in the repo, but the README does not state which flags produced the tables; the 16 B and 10 kB rows need -v overrides and, given the 18.6m figure, a large -b batch (pipelining).
corrections.caveats: Tier C: first-party README numbers with no CPU model, core count, kernel version, Redis or memcached version, connection count, pipelining/batch size or run command stated. The bench/bench.go harness in the repo defaults to 16 connections, batch 1, a 16-byte key and a 256-byte value, and issues GET on one single key (zero-filled key and value) over and over, so the hot path is one cache-resident entry and the result mostly measures the network loop, not the hash index. At batch 1, 18.6m ops/sec over 16 TCP connections would need sub-microsecond round trips, so the headline row was almost certainly run with heavy pipelining that the README does not disclose. bench.go only speaks mrcache's binary protocol and Redis RESP; it has no memcached mode, and bench/py/mc.py, red.py and mrc.py are one-shot set/get smoke scripts, so the harness behind the memcached numbers is not in the repo. The client counts a batch complete after length*batch bytes, which undercounts both servers' replies (mrcache sends a 4-byte length header plus the value per GET; a Redis RESP bulk reply adds 7 bytes at 16 B and 10 bytes at 10 kB), so split reads can let the client run ahead of its replies and the per-server error differs. Numbers moved between README revisions: 1.07m vs redis 270k vs memcached 100k (commit cce89a1, 2024-02-28; 10 kB rows 179k / 79k zstd / memcached 24k / redis 32k), 9.8m vs 2.7m vs 400k (commit e33dfb6, 2024-04-21), 18.6m vs 2.5m vs 400k (from 2024-04-24, after the io_uring multishot rewrite); the 10 kB rows are identical in e33dfb6 and HEAD, so they predate the rewrite. The headline '25x faster than memcached' is stale against the current table (18.6m/400k is about 46x, derived from page data). The server uses io_uring SQPOLL, which keeps a kernel polling thread busy on an extra core; Redis in its default configuration runs commands on one thread and memcached defaults to 4 worker threads, so per-core fairness is unstated. Single-node in-memory scope only; no networked or persistence comparison. The README is inconsistent on the kernel requirement (5.5+ in the intro, 5.8+ in Dependencies) and the HEAD Makefile still links -lmrloop although mrloop.h was removed on 2024-05-12 and the README no longer lists mrloop, so a build may need fixes. No third-party measurement found (WebSearch for mrcache with io_uring, Redis and memcached returned nothing about the project).

notes: README numbers match the record; repo metadata checked (MIT, 26 stars, 2 forks, not archived or a fork, last commit 2024-10-29 'Add Liburing dependency to the README', so stale). Corrections only sharpen the harness caveats: bench.go defaults to a 256-byte value, undercounts mrcache's 4-byte reply header as well as Redis RESP framing, and the 18.6m row implies undisclosed pipelining. Shortcomings to record: unstated hardware/versions/run flags, memcached harness missing, single-key loopback workload, SQPOLL extra core, stale 25x headline.
